```sh
git clone git@github.com:bar9/yolo-twice.git
cd yolo-twice/code
bun install          # all workspaces, about 2 s
bun run build        # core, analyzers, engine, pele-markdown, then the UI, about 10 s
bun test             # 22 tests, about 2 s
bun run typecheck
```

Start the engine for this repository and open the UI:

```sh
bun run cli open --cwd ..      # starts the daemon if needed, prints and opens the URL
bun run cli status --cwd ..
bun run cli stop
```

The repository ships its own `.yolo-twice/` folder, so even on a machine that never ran a
session here the UI shows the committed history. To continue that session in Claude Code:

```sh
bun run cli resume --cwd ..    # rebuilds the transcript under ~/.claude and runs claude --resume
```

## Running the plugin from your checkout

Two options, pick one.

**Per session, nothing installed.** Claude Code loads the plugin straight from the folder:

```sh
cd /path/to/yolo-twice
claude --plugin-dir code/plugin
```

**Installed, the way users get it.** Register your checkout as a local marketplace once.
Edits to the plugin files take effect in new sessions:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add /path/to/yolo-twice
claude plugin install yolo-twice@yolo-twice
```

Inside Claude Code the command is `/yolo-twice:yolo-twice`, with `stop`, `status`,
`mode <detent>` and `resume [id]`. The plugin's launcher finds the engine in your checkout,
so it runs your local code. It prefers `code/packages/engine/dist/cli.js` when present, so
run `bun run build` after changing engine code, or delete `dist/` to fall back to running
the TypeScript source with bun.

Hooks post to `127.0.0.1:9656`. When the engine is down they fail silently, so a session
without the engine is never disturbed.

To remove the dev install:

```sh
claude plugin uninstall yolo-twice@yolo-twice
claude plugin marketplace remove yolo-twice
```

## Where the code lives

| Path | What | Inner loop |
|---|---|---|
### Engine

Run it in the foreground from source so logs go to your terminal:

```sh
bun run engine -- --cwd ..
```

Useful environment variables:

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `YOLO_TWICE_PORT` | port instead of 9656, so a dev engine can run next to an installed one |
| `YOLO_TWICE_HOME` | runtime state folder instead of `~/.yolo-twice` |
| `YOLO_TWICE_NO_LLM=1` | never call `claude -p`; summaries come from the structural fallback |
| `YOLO_TWICE_ORIGIN_DIR` | `index` reads sessions from this folder instead of `~/.claude/projects/<slug>` |
| `YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE` | the plugin launcher runs this engine (a `cli.js`, a `cli.ts` or a command) |
| `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | where Claude Code's data lives, if not `~/.claude` |

A fully isolated dev engine that cannot collide with anything installed:

```sh
YOLO_TWICE_HOME=/tmp/yt-home YOLO_TWICE_PORT=9661 YOLO_TWICE_NO_LLM=1 bun run engine -- --cwd ..
```

Stop the npx engine that's holding port 9656, then start the engine from source in `code/`. The hooks always post to port 9656, so whichever engine owns that port is the one that receives your sessions.

## 1. Free port 9656

The engine you have running now came from npm (started with `npx`) and is watching `/home/bar9/testing`. Stop it:

```sh
npx yolo-twice stop      # or: kill 815368
```

## 2. Build and run from source

```sh
cd /home/bar9/yolo-twice/code
bun install
bun run build
bun run engine -- --cwd ..     # runs in the foreground, logs go to your terminal
```

To start it in the background instead and open the UI, run `bun run cli open --cwd ..`.

## 3. Make `/yolo-twice:yolo-twice` use your checkout

Without this step, the slash command can start the npm engine again. Your installed plugin is 0.1.0 from the GitHub marketplace, so it doesn't know where your checkout is. Pick one fix:

- **Per session:** start Claude with `claude --plugin-dir code/plugin` from the repo root.
- **Permanently:** switch the marketplace to your local folder:

## Running a test engine alongside the real one

If you want to try out engine changes without disturbing the engine that records your sessions, run a second one on another port with its own state folder. With `YOLO_TWICE_NO_LLM=1` it never calls `claude -p`:

```sh
YOLO_TWICE_HOME=/tmp/yt-home YOLO_TWICE_PORT=9661 YOLO_TWICE_NO_LLM=1 bun run engine -- --cwd ..
```

These steps come from `CONTRIBUTING.md` (the "Running the plugin from your checkout" and "Engine" sections).

== bin/yolo-twice
#!/bin/sh
# Run the yolo-twice engine CLI. Resolution order:
#   1. $YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE  (path to cli.js, or a command)
#   2. repo dev layout next to this plugin (code/packages/engine)
#   3. a marketplace clone under ~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/*/code/packages/engine (built on first use with bun)
#   4. npx -y yolo-twice@latest
set -u
HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
CMD="${1:-open}"; [ $# -gt 0 ] && shift
case "$CMD" in
  stop|status|index|start|open|mode|resume|hook|help) ;;
  micro|attentive|balanced|yolo) set -- "$CMD" "$@"; CMD=mode ;;
  *) set -- "$CMD" "$@"; CMD=open ;;
esac

run_engine_dir() {
  dir="$1"; shift
  if [ -f "$dir/dist/cli.js" ]; then exec node "$dir/dist/cli.js" "$@"; fi
  if command -v bun >/dev/null 2>&1 && [ -f "$dir/src/cli.ts" ]; then
    if [ ! -d "$dir/../../node_modules" ]; then (cd "$dir/../.." && bun install >/dev/null 2>&1); fi
    exec bun run "$dir/src/cli.ts" "$@"
  fi
  return 1
}

if [ -n "${YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE:-}" ]; then
  case "$YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE" in
    *.js) exec node "$YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE" "$CMD" "$@" ;;
    *.ts) exec bun run "$YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE" "$CMD" "$@" ;;
    *) exec "$YOLO_TWICE_ENGINE" "$CMD" "$@" ;;
  esac
fi
if [ -d "$HERE/../packages/engine" ]; then run_engine_dir "$HERE/../packages/engine" "$CMD" "$@"; fi
CLAUDE_DIR="${CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR:-$HOME/.claude}"
for d in "$CLAUDE_DIR"/plugins/marketplaces/*/code/packages/engine; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && run_engine_dir "$d" "$CMD" "$@"
done
# marketplace added from a local directory (dev install): its path is recorded in known_marketplaces.json
if [ -f "$CLAUDE_DIR/plugins/known_marketplaces.json" ]; then
  for p in $(grep -o '"path": *"[^"]*"' "$CLAUDE_DIR/plugins/known_marketplaces.json" | sed 's/.*"path": *"//; s/"$//'); do
    [ -d "$p/code/packages/engine" ] && run_engine_dir "$p/code/packages/engine" "$CMD" "$@"
  done
fi
exec npx -y yolo-twice@latest "$CMD" "$@"

# yolo-twice **Transparent agentic development superpowers.** See what your coding agent did, at the zoom level you choose, while it is still running. ## The problem A long Claude Code session leaves behind megabytes of JSONL: hundreds of turns, tool calls, subagent transcripts, rewinds and compactions. Reading it as a chat list does not scale, and the existing viewers, good as they are, show exactly that list. You either micro-manage every tool call or you go full yolo and lose track of what happened. ## What yolo-twice does - **Semantic zoom.** Read a session as one line, three sentences, a paragraph of phases, the turns, or the raw records. Any text, including the top summary and a long tool result, can be zoomed out one more step or expanded in place. - **Live flow graph.** The conversation as a graph: turns, tool calls, subagents and rewind branches, updated while the session runs, merging into phases as you zoom out. - **Attention slider.** From "micro management" (every turn summarized live) to "yolo" (nothing until you ask, then "catch me up"). You choose how many tokens and how much attention to spend; the cost is shown next to the slider. - **Linked views, shareable links.** Filter bar, timeline, reader and graph react to each other: drag a time window, double click to zoom into a phase or turn, filter to your prompts or tool errors, and every view follows. The URL captures the whole view, so a link opens exactly what you saw. - **Project-local history.** Everything derived lands in `.yolo-twice/` in your repo, redacted, plain JSON and mermaid, so you can commit it or gitignore it. - **Incremental and idempotent.** Stop the engine, resume later, run it twice: same bytes. ## Install One command, in a terminal where Claude Code is installed (version 2.1.275 or newer, Node 22 or newer): ``` claude plugin install yolo-twice --marketplace /yolo-twice ``` ## Use Inside any Claude Code session (plugin commands are namespaced, so the command is `/yolo-twice:yolo-twice`): ``` /yolo-twice:yolo-twice start the engine for this project and open the UI /yolo-twice:yolo-twice stop stop the engine /yolo-twice:yolo-twice status show engine, session and index state /yolo-twice:yolo-twice mode yolo set the attention slider: micro | attentive | balanced | yolo /yolo-twice:yolo-twice resume [id] rebuild a committed session's transcript and print the claude --resume command ``` The same commands work from a terminal via the engine CLI, for example `yolo-twice status` or `yolo-twice index` for a one-shot index without the daemon. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR CC[Claude Code session] -- "hooks" --> ENG[Engine] CC -- writes --> JSONL[(session JSONL
+ subagents)] JSONL -- "incremental read" --> ENG ENG --> NORM[normalize + redact] NORM --> STORE[(.yolo-twice/)] STORE --> AN[analyzers
structure, search, claude -p] AN --> STORE ENG -- "HTTP + SSE" --> UI[web UI
zoom, graph, timeline, search] ``` Claude Code hooks tell the engine that something happened. The engine reads the new lines of the session transcript from its cursor, normalizes them into one event per line, redacts secrets, and appends them to `.yolo-twice/`. Structural levels (session, phases, turns, steps) are derived without any model call. Summaries and labels are produced by the Claude Code CLI itself in headless mode, cached by content hash, and only as eagerly as the attention slider allows. The UI is updated over Server-Sent Events. ```mermaid flowchart TB P[Project digest] --- S[Session title] S --- A[Abstract: 3 sentences] A --- PH[Phases] PH --- T[Turns] T --- ST[Steps: tool calls, thinking, subagents] ST --- R[Raw records] ``` ## What lands in your repo ``` .yolo-twice/ config.json team settings: redaction rules, analyzers, default attention sessions// meta.json label, time span, size and cost of the session events.ndjson redacted, normalized events structure.json the zoom tree graph.mmd the flow graph as mermaid text/ titles, abstracts and summaries of finished parts cache/, local.json gitignored: project list, cursors, live summaries, your slider ``` Every committed file belongs to exactly one session, so teammates indexing in parallel never produce merge conflicts in this folder. Raw transcripts stay in `~/.claude`. Only redacted events and derived data are written here. Paths are written portably: the project root as `$PROJECT`, your home folder as `~`, your login name as ``. Nobody's username or folder layout ends up in the repo. Because the redacted events are complete, a teammate who clones the repo can continue a session that never ran on their machine: `yolo-twice resume` rebuilds the Claude Code transcript from `events.ndjson` with paths expanded to their own machine and continues it with `claude --resume --fork-session`, as a new session of their own. ## Acknowledgments yolo-twice did not invent transcript viewing. These projects came first, and we learned from each of them. If one of them fits your need better, use it. | Project | What it does well | Where yolo-twice differs | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | [Claudescope](https://github.com/vladar107/claudescope) by vladar107 | Browses eight agents, full-text search, cost analytics, MCP server and plugin | Abstraction levels, flow graph, committed project history | | [claude-code-history-viewer](https://github.com/jhlee0409/claude-code-history-viewer) by jhlee0409 | Desktop app for over thirty agents, live updates, session board | One running session, deeply zoomable, instead of breadth | .yolo-twice: cache config.json sessions .yolo-twice/sessions/34b27ceb-5af1-4142-8334-ab80a4310636/: events.ndjson graph.L1.mmd graph.mmd meta.json structure.json text .yolo-twice/sessions/5fb80521-9a5e-4652-a91f-b5fdecabb9fd/: events.ndjson graph.L1.mmd graph.mmd structure.json .yolo-twice/sessions/7f825bc9-97c2-4932-8575-d8beab55a0eb/: events.ndjson graph.L1.mmd graph.mmd structure.json text # runtime state, never commit cache/ engine.json local.json

The deck covers story and impact well, but it barely touches three things judges score: technical depth, code quality and fair play. Of all the criteria, the demo is the one most at risk.

| Criterion | How the deck covers it |
|---|---|
| Innovation | Partly |

## Innovation: partly covered
**The core idea stands out, but the deck never says what's new.** "Treat agent interaction as code" is a real value proposition, and the deck makes it concrete (slide 5, the `git show`). But when we removed the comparison table, we also removed the sentence saying why this differs from existing viewers. Now only the thanks slide mentions them, as credits.
- **Fix:** add one line to slide 5, something like *"Existing viewers show you the transcript. We put it in the repository and make it readable at any level of detail."*

## Impact: partly covered
**Slide 8 covers impact on a team, but not the wider social and economic relevance the criterion asks for.** What's missing is *why now*: AI agents write more and more of the code, and people need to be able to trust it, check it, and keep knowing why it was written that way. It's also missing the economic side: review time, onboarding, and knowledge lost when people leave.
- **Fix:** add one closing sentence to slide 8 along those lines. Leave out invented numbers, which would undercut the honest tone.

## Technical depth: weak
**Making the deck accessible stripped out almost all the engineering, and judges score exactly that.** None of this appears on a slide:
- the engine reads incrementally and gives identical output every time it runs
- secrets are removed before anything is written
- the structure is derived without an AI model
- summaries are written on demand and cached by content
- the attention slider controls cost
- `resume` rebuilds a working transcript on another machine
- 50 tests and 343 assertions pass (I just ran them)
- **Fix:** add a compact "Under the hood" slide after slide 7. Tag its points for developers so managers can skip it, or keep it as a backup slide for questions.

## AI code review: missing, and the history has weak spots
**The deck says nothing about code quality, and the commit history has spots an AI reviewer will flag.**
- **Commit messages:** two say only "yolo" and "moro yolo".
- **Very large early commits:** the first three are a minute apart and each finishes a whole track (engine, CLI, plugin, then the complete web UI).
- **On the plus side:** tests, typecheck and CI all exist.

**Our unique advantage:** the AI sessions that wrote the code are committed next to it, so a reviewer can read *why* the code looks the way it does. That's our own pitch applied to our own repo.
- **Fix:** on slide 9, say explicitly that the build sessions are committed and can be reviewed, and mention the tests. Write clear commit messages from now on. I wouldn't rewrite shared history on `main`.

## Fair play: missing, with a risk
**Judges reading the history will see complete tracks at 10:18–10:21 on Saturday, which can look like code prepared before the event.** I don't know how that work was actually done: maybe parallel sessions that were squashed into single commits, or design done in advance. You and the team need to have a clear answer ready.
- **The committed sessions are your strongest evidence,** because they carry timestamps showing when the work happened. That only holds if they really cover the build. Only the original build session (`34b27ceb`) is still in the repo, and the other team members' sessions may not be.
- **Already handled:** credit to the earlier projects. Consider also stating where the cover art came from (AI-generated or not).

## Pitch: strong
**The story is clear and honest, and it runs to 3:00.** It goes from scene to problem to idea, how it works, impact and demo. Slides 4 and 8 mirror each other, which gives a strong, memorable structure.
- **The only risk is delivery.** The speaker notes are written out in full, so rehearse them once, not read from them.

## Demo: at risk
**Slide 9 hands over to the demo well, but the deck doesn't plan what to show, and nothing protects against failure.** The story promises a payoff: find the moment a decision was made and share a link to it. The demo session is the yolo-twice build session, not the login story, so pick one real decision in it in advance and show that same path: one-line summary → chapter → the decision → copy the link.
- **Fix:** write that exact click path into the slide 9 notes. Prepare a fallback, such as screenshots or a short screen recording, in case the engine or the Wi-Fi fails. Restart the engine and open the UI just before going on stage.

Four edits, together less than a minute of extra talk:
1. **Slide 5:** add the "what's new" line (innovation).
2. **Slide 8:** add the "why it matters beyond one team" line (impact).

4. **Slide 9:** add the committed sessions as evidence, plus tests and CI (code review and fair play), and a demo click path and fallback in the notes.

## The problem

An AI agent works for three hours. The pull request is +2,400 lines. A reviewer asks a fair

The answer exists. Claude Code keeps a readable transcript of every session. But three hours

decision, and it stays on the laptop where it ran. For the rest of the team the session is a

review sees the code but never the conversation that produced it.

reviewed.

## The idea: keep the conversation with the code

removes secrets, and saves it in the project as plain files: versioned, shareable, reviewable
and resumable. One change, one commit: the code, and the conversation that produced it.

Then it makes the session readable. Start from one line, open three sentences, then the
chapters, a single exchange, or the raw log. Or look at the session as a map, where every
detour, helper agent and change of plan stays visible.

```
/yolo-twice:yolo-twice                  start the engine for this project and open the UI
/yolo-twice:yolo-twice stop             stop the engine

/yolo-twice:yolo-twice autocommit on    commit only .yolo-twice every 10 minutes, for this engine run
/yolo-twice:yolo-twice resume [id]      continue a committed session on this machine, as a fork
```

The same commands work from a terminal through the engine CLI, for example

## What lands in your repo

```
.yolo-twice/
  config.json                  team settings: redaction rules, analyzers, default attention
  sessions/<id>/
    meta.json                  label, time span, size and cost of the session
    events.ndjson              redacted, normalized events
    structure.json             the zoom tree

    text/                      titles, abstracts and summaries of finished parts
    images/                    images pasted into prompts, shown in the reader
  cache/, local.json           gitignored: project list, cursors, live summaries, your slider
```

Commit it to share the history with your team, or add `.yolo-twice/` to `.gitignore`. Every
committed file belongs to exactly one session, so teammates indexing in parallel never get
merge conflicts in this folder. `autocommit on` commits only this folder, never your code.

`claude --resume <file> --fork-session` command that continues it as a new session of their own.

assignments; long tool results are truncated to head and tail with a hash. Add your own
patterns in `config.json`.

login name as `<user>`. Nobody's username or folder layout ends up in the repo.

{"file_path":"$PROJECT/code/site/attention.md","content":"# Attention slider: micro management to yolo

Not every layer costs the same. Ingestion, redaction, the structural tree and the search index
are cheap and incremental, so they always run near realtime and the data is always complete.
Semantic analysis through `claude -p` is the expensive layer: seconds per call, thousands of
tokens, and it competes with your own session for the same subscription rate limit.
Re-summarizing a part of the session that is still growing, after every turn, costs tokens
again and again.

The slider therefore decides only **which summaries the engine writes ahead of time**. It
never affects ingestion, and it never limits what you can read: any summary the slider skips
is written when you open that node in the reader.

## The four detents

A part of the session is *closed* once newer work follows it, or once the session has been
idle for 30 minutes. The newest turn and the newest phase are *open* while the session runs.

| Detent | Written ahead of time | Lag of the summaries | Rough cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Micro management | Title and abstract of every turn and every phase, and of the session, including the open ones, refreshed as they grow | seconds | ≈ 3 calls per turn |
| Attentive | A title for every closed turn; title and abstract for every closed phase | about one turn | ≈ 1 call per turn |
| Balanced (default) | Title and abstract for every closed phase | about one phase | ≈ 1 call per 4 turns |
| Yolo | Nothing | on demand | only what you open |

Phases are split structurally, without a model: at compactions, after long idle gaps, and at
prompts that change the topic.

## Design rules

- **The reader is the demand signal.** Whatever the detent, opening a node that has no summary
  yet asks the engine for one. The slider only decides how much is ready before you look.
- **Short text is never summarized.** A one-line prompt or a single tool call is already as
  short as a title, so it is shown as it is, without a model call.
- **Same input, same summary.** Every summary is keyed by the hash of its input text, the
  granularity and the analyzer. A closed phase has the same input in every mode, so its summary
  is identical whether it was written eagerly or on demand, and it is only written once.
- **Open parts stay local.** Summaries of turns and phases that are still growing go to the
  gitignored `.yolo-twice/cache/`, never into the committed `sessions/` folder.
- **The cost is shown next to the slider**, as an estimate of summarization calls per hour for
  the current session, together with the expected lag.
- **The setting is personal.** The team default is `attention` in `.yolo-twice/config.json`
  (balanced). Your own choice lives in the gitignored `.yolo-twice/local.json` and can be
  changed live from the UI or with `/yolo-twice:yolo-twice mode <micro|attentive|balanced|yolo>`.
- **The model is configurable.** All summaries use the model set in `analyzers.model` in
  `config.json` (default: haiku), whatever the detent.

## Catch me up

The "Catch me up" button summarizes everything that happened in the session since this
browser last showed it. It is most useful in yolo mode: let the agent work, come back, and
read one paragraph instead of the whole transcript. The position is remembered per session in
the browser, so each viewer gets their own "since you last looked".

## 6. Attention slider: micro management to yolo

Not every layer costs the same. Ingestion, redaction, the structural tree and the search index
are cheap and incremental, so they always run near realtime and the data is always complete.
Semantic analysis through `claude -p` is the expensive layer: seconds to minutes per call,
thousands of tokens, and it competes with the user's own session for the same subscription
rate limit. Re-summarizing an open phase after every turn is quadratic in tokens and every
interim result is a cache miss by design.

The slider therefore controls semantic triggers and UI attention, never ingestion. Four
detents, not a continuous value, so each mode is testable:

| Micro management | every turn: incremental fold summary of the open phase, small model | L3 steps | live ticker, graph re-layout batched to 1 s |
| Attentive | turn label on each Stop hook, phase summary when the phase closes | L2 turns | live, no interim phase summaries |
| Balanced (default) | phase close only: compaction, idle gap, topic change | L1 phases | updates on phase boundaries |
| Yolo | nothing automatic; summaries computed lazily for nodes the UI shows, or on SessionEnd | L0 digest | "catch me up": digest of everything since the user last looked |

Design rules:

- The UI viewport is the demand signal. The UI requests summaries for visible nodes; the
  slider only sets how far ahead the engine prefetches. One code path, different policy.
- Idempotency survives the slider. A closed phase has the same input hash in every mode, so
  its artifact is identical whether computed eagerly or lazily. Interim summaries of open
  phases carry `interim: true` and live in `cache/`, never in the committed `sessions/`.
